text.ch-anatomy:
CHAPTER 1 OF 5 · FACE BLOCKS

Anatomy: the trigeminal nerve

The trigeminal ganglion lies in Meckel’s cave, near the apex of the petrous temporal bone. Three divisions leave it:

Ophthalmic (V1), sensory: through the superior orbital fissure into the orbit. Forehead, upper eyelid and the front of the nose.
Maxillary (V2), sensory: through the foramen rotundum and the pterygopalatine fossa, to the face through the infraorbital foramen. Lower eyelid, cheek, side of the nose, upper lip, upper teeth, palate and maxillary sinus.
Mandibular (V3), sensory and motor (muscles of mastication): through the foramen ovale. The temple and front of the ear, the front two-thirds of the tongue, the lower teeth and the skin over the mandible.

Each can be blocked where it leaves the skull (V2 and V3, deep) or, more simply, where its end branches leave the facial bones (V1, V2, V3, superficial).

Three foramina in one line
1
2
3
Front (right side shaded)
Supraorbital notch (V1): on the upper orbital rim. Block
Infraorbital foramen (V2): about 1 cm below the lower orbital rim. Block
Mental foramen (V3): below the second premolar. Block

All three lie on a vertical line through the pupil when the patient looks straight ahead. Fill patterns here separate the territories: solid supraorbital and mental, hatched supratrochlear and infraorbital.

EXAM PEARL

Five blocks for the whole face

Supraorbital, supratrochlear, infraorbital and mental blocks on both sides, with the auriculotemporal and great auricular nerves for the sides, cover the skin of almost the whole face.

CHAPTER 2 OF 5 · FACE · V1

Supraorbital and supratrochlear nerve blocks

The two branches of the frontal nerve (V1) leave the orbit over the upper orbital rim: the supraorbital nerve through its notch in line with the pupil, the supratrochlear nerve about 1 cm medial to it. Between them they supply the forehead and the scalp back to the vertex.

USE IT FOR

Forehead and frontal scalp lacerations and lesions
Frontal craniotomy (part of a scalp block)
Frontal headache (pain clinic)

PROBE
Linear, transverse along the eyebrow
NEEDLE
25–27G
DOSE
1–2 ml per nerve
COVERS

Simulated image drawn by this page, not a patient scan. Use the arrow keys on the image to step through.

Position

Supine, head in the midline. Ask the patient to look straight ahead so you can line up the pupil.

Equipment
High-frequency linear probe (a small “hockey stick” probe fits the face best)
25–27G needle
1–2 ml of local anaesthetic per nerve, with or without adrenaline
Landmarks and scanning

Feel the supraorbital notch on the upper orbital rim in line with the pupil, and inject just above it. Then move 1 cm medially, to the bridge of the nose, for the supratrochlear nerve. On ultrasound, the notch is a gap in the bright bone line with the supraorbital artery pulsing in it.

Needle approach

A fine needle to the tissue just outside the foramen, in-plane or out-of-plane. Never inject into the foramen or canal: the nerve is trapped in bone there, so an intraneural injection is more likely.

Sonoanatomy

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Frontalis and orbicularis oculi
Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

1–2 ml of local anaesthetic per nerve

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Coverage

Front

Right side

Dense: reliable
One side shown (the patient’s right). Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Supraorbital (V1): forehead and scalp back to the vertex
Supratrochlear (V1): the middle of the forehead

Covers: The forehead and scalp back to the vertex, on one side.

MECHANISM

Both nerves are superficial as they cross the orbital rim, so a small volume reaches them.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Reliable for skin surgery. Block both sides for a midline wound.

WHAT IT MISSES
The temple (zygomaticotemporal and auriculotemporal nerves).
The nose below the bridge (external nasal and infraorbital nerves).
Complications and how to avoid them
Bruising and swelling, the commonest problems: use a fine needle and press afterwards.
Intravascular injection: each nerve travels with an artery. Aspirate. Arteries of the face run to the brain, so even small volumes can cause toxicity.
Nerve injury from injecting into the foramen.
Practical pearls
Keep a finger on the orbital rim: the needle stays above it.
One puncture can reach both: inject at the notch, then fan 1 cm medially.

CHAPTER 3 OF 5 · FACE · V2

Infraorbital nerve block

The infraorbital nerve, the end of the maxillary nerve (V2), leaves the infraorbital foramen about 1 cm below the lower orbital rim, in line with the pupil. It supplies the lower eyelid, the cheek, the side of the nose and the upper lip.

Cleft lip repair in children (both sides)
Upper lip and nose surgery, lacerations
Endoscopic sinus and nasal surgery (part of multimodal analgesia)

PROBE

NEEDLE
25–27G; extraoral or intraoral
DOSE
1–2 ml (adult)
COVERS
Lower lid, cheek, side of the nose, upper lip

Position

Equipment

Landmarks and scanning

Feel the foramen about 1 cm below the middle of the lower orbital rim, in line with the pupil. Extraoral: insert the needle just below it, keeping a finger on the orbital rim. Intraoral: lift the upper lip and insert the needle in the gum–lip fold above the canine or first premolar, aiming up towards the finger on the foramen. On ultrasound, the foramen is a gap in the bright maxilla.

Needle approach

A fine needle to the tissue just outside the foramen, in-plane or out-of-plane. Never inject into the foramen or canal: the nerve is trapped in bone there, so an intraneural injection is more likely.

Sonoanatomy

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Levator labii superioris
Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

1–2 ml of local anaesthetic per side (adult)

Less in children: use a weight-based dose.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Coverage

Front

Right side

Dense: reliable
One side shown (the patient’s right). Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Infraorbital (V2): lower eyelid, cheek, side of the nose and upper lip

Covers: Lower eyelid, cheek, side of the nose and upper lip on one side.

MECHANISM

The nerve fans out to the face as soon as it leaves the foramen, so one injection at the foramen covers all its branches.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Reliable for skin and lip surgery. Bilateral infraorbital blocks are widely used for cleft lip repair in children; trials suggest better analgesia than opioids alone, but the evidence is low quality.

WHAT IT MISSES
The teeth and gums of the upper jaw beyond the front teeth, and the palate (other branches of V2, given off before the foramen).
The midline of the lip, unless both sides are blocked.
Complications and how to avoid them
Bruising and swelling, the commonest problems: use a fine needle and press afterwards.
Intravascular injection: each nerve travels with an artery. Aspirate. Arteries of the face run to the brain, so even small volumes can cause toxicity.
Nerve injury from injecting into the foramen.
Practical pearls
A finger on the orbital rim protects the eye.
For cleft lip, block both sides.

text.ch-deep:
CHAPTER 5 OF 5 · FACE · DEEP TRIGEMINAL

Maxillary and mandibular nerve blocks

Blocks of the whole V2 or V3 division close to the skull base, in the pterygopalatine fossa (V2) or just below the foramen ovale (V3). Deep, close to the maxillary artery, and not for beginners: learn them with an experienced colleague.

1
2
Right side
Suprazygomatic approach to V2: the angle between the upper border of the zygomatic arch and the back of the lateral orbital rim.
Infrazygomatic (coronoid notch) approach to V2 or V3: below the middle of the zygomatic arch, between the coronoid process and the condyle of the mandible.

Shading: V2 territory hatched (infraorbital and zygomaticotemporal), V3 solid (auriculotemporal and mental). Schematic.

Maxillary nerve (V2): suprazygomatic approach

Covers the upper jaw, upper teeth, palate, the side of the nose, the cheek and the upper lip. Its main use is cleft palate repair in children.

The needle enters at the frontozygomatic angle, goes perpendicular to the skin until it touches the greater wing of the sphenoid, then is turned downwards and forwards into the pterygopalatine fossa.
With ultrasound, the probe lies below the zygomatic arch over the maxilla to watch the fossa; the needle is seen out of plane, and spread was seen in almost every block in one series of infants.
In a randomised trial in infants, bilateral blocks with 0.15 ml/kg of 0.2% ropivacaine per side halved morphine use in the 48 hours after cleft palate repair.
Mandibular nerve (V3): coronoid notch approach

Covers the lower jaw and teeth, the front two-thirds of the tongue, the floor of the mouth, the temple and the front of the ear, and relaxes the muscles of mastication. Used for jaw and tongue surgery and in the pain clinic (trigeminal neuralgia).

The needle enters in the coronoid notch, below the middle of the zygomatic arch, perpendicular to the skin, to the lateral pterygoid plate. It is then walked off the back of the plate for V3, or the front of it (towards the pterygopalatine fossa) for V2.
Aspirate often: the maxillary artery is in the way. The pharynx is just medial.
RISK	WHY
Intravascular injection, haematoma
Maxillary artery and pterygoid venous plexus. Arterial blood from here goes to the brain: small volumes can cause seizures.
Spread into the orbit
From the pterygopalatine fossa through the inferior orbital fissure: transient diplopia or visual loss (V2).
Subarachnoid spread
Rare: a needle advanced too far, towards the foramen ovale or the skull base.
Pharyngeal puncture
A needle advanced too deep, medial to the pterygoid plate.

General complications of head and neck blocks: high spinal or brainstem anaesthesia; intravascular injection and toxicity (0.5 ml or less into an artery can cause a seizure); bruising; and airway problems from block of the phrenic or recurrent laryngeal nerves.

STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

Probe transverse along the eyebrow, over the upper orbital rim. Slide medially and laterally until the bright bone line has a gap: the supraorbital notch or foramen, usually in line with the pupil.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

Skin, fat, the thin frontalis and orbicularis oculi, then the bright frontal bone with its shadow. The supraorbital artery pulses at the notch (colour Doppler); the nerve lies beside it.

In-plane from lateral (or out-of-plane), a fine needle to the tissue just over the notch. Do not enter the foramen.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

1–2 ml. Then press on the site. For the supratrochlear nerve, add 1 ml just medial, at the bridge of the nose (or fan medially from the same puncture).

CHAPTER 3 OF 5 · FACE · V2

Infraorbital nerve block

The infraorbital nerve, the end of the maxillary nerve (V2), leaves the infraorbital foramen about 1 cm below the lower orbital rim, in line with the pupil. It supplies the lower eyelid, the cheek, the side of the nose and the upper lip.

USE IT FOR

Cleft lip repair in children (both sides)
Upper lip and nose surgery, lacerations
Endoscopic sinus and nasal surgery (part of multimodal analgesia)
POSITION
Supine, looking ahead
PROBE
Linear, transverse below the orbital rim
NEEDLE
25–27G; extraoral or intraoral
DOSE
1–2 ml (adult)
COVERS
Lower lid, cheek, side of the nose, upper lip

Simulated image drawn by this page, not a patient scan. Use the arrow keys on the image to step through.

Position

Supine, head in the midline. Ask the patient to look straight ahead so you can line up the pupil.

Equipment
High-frequency linear probe (a small “hockey stick” probe fits the face best)
25–27G needle
1–2 ml of local anaesthetic per nerve, with or without adrenaline
Landmarks and scanning

Feel the foramen about 1 cm below the middle of the lower orbital rim, in line with the pupil. Extraoral: insert the needle just below it, keeping a finger on the orbital rim. Intraoral: lift the upper lip and insert the needle in the gum–lip fold above the canine or first premolar, aiming up towards the finger on the foramen. On ultrasound, the foramen is a gap in the bright maxilla.

Needle approach

A fine needle to the tissue just outside the foramen, in-plane or out-of-plane. Never inject into the foramen or canal: the nerve is trapped in bone there, so an intraneural injection is more likely.

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Levator labii superioris
Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

1–2 ml of local anaesthetic per side (adult)

Less in children: use a weight-based dose.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Coverage

Front

Right side

Dense: reliable
One side shown (the patient’s right). Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Infraorbital (V2): lower eyelid, cheek, side of the nose and upper lip

Covers: Lower eyelid, cheek, side of the nose and upper lip on one side.

MECHANISM

The nerve fans out to the face as soon as it leaves the foramen, so one injection at the foramen covers all its branches.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Reliable for skin and lip surgery. Bilateral infraorbital blocks are widely used for cleft lip repair in children; trials suggest better analgesia than opioids alone, but the evidence is low quality.

WHAT IT MISSES
The teeth and gums of the upper jaw beyond the front teeth, and the palate (other branches of V2, given off before the foramen).
The midline of the lip, unless both sides are blocked.
Complications and how to avoid them
Bruising and swelling, the commonest problems: use a fine needle and press afterwards.
Intravascular injection: each nerve travels with an artery. Aspirate. Arteries of the face run to the brain, so even small volumes can cause toxicity.
Nerve injury from injecting into the foramen.
Practical pearls
A finger on the orbital rim protects the eye.
For cleft lip, block both sides.

Landmarks and scanning

The foramen is below the second premolar, halfway between the gum and the lower border of the mandible, in line with the pupil. Intraoral: insert the needle in the gum–lip fold at the second premolar. On ultrasound, the foramen is a gap in the bright mandible.

Needle approach

A fine needle to the tissue just outside the foramen, in-plane or out-of-plane. Never inject into the foramen or canal: the nerve is trapped in bone there, so an intraneural injection is more likely.

MECHANISM

As for the infraorbital nerve: one injection at the foramen covers the branches to the lip and chin.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Reliable for skin. The lower teeth are not covered (they are supplied inside the bone, before the foramen).

WHAT IT MISSES
The lower teeth and the tongue.
The other side of the lip.
Complications and how to avoid them
Bruising and swelling, the commonest problems: use a fine needle and press afterwards.
Intravascular injection: each nerve travels with an artery. Aspirate. Arteries of the face run to the brain, so even small volumes can cause toxicity.
Nerve injury from injecting into the foramen.

text.ch-deep:
CHAPTER 5 OF 5 · FACE · DEEP TRIGEMINAL

Maxillary and mandibular nerve blocks

Blocks of the whole V2 or V3 division close to the skull base, in the pterygopalatine fossa (V2) or just below the foramen ovale (V3). Deep, close to the maxillary artery, and not for beginners: learn them with an experienced colleague.

1
2
Right side
Suprazygomatic approach to V2: the angle between the upper border of the zygomatic arch and the back of the lateral orbital rim.
Infrazygomatic (coronoid notch) approach to V2 or V3: below the middle of the zygomatic arch, between the coronoid process and the condyle of the mandible.

Shading: V2 territory hatched (infraorbital and zygomaticotemporal), V3 solid (auriculotemporal and mental). Schematic.

Maxillary nerve (V2): suprazygomatic approach

Covers the upper jaw, upper teeth, palate, the side of the nose, the cheek and the upper lip. Its main use is cleft palate repair in children.

The needle enters at the frontozygomatic angle, goes perpendicular to the skin until it touches the greater wing of the sphenoid, then is turned downwards and forwards into the pterygopalatine fossa.
With ultrasound, the probe lies below the zygomatic arch over the maxilla to watch the fossa; the needle is seen out of plane, and spread was seen in almost every block in one series of infants.
In a randomised trial in infants, bilateral blocks with 0.15 ml/kg of 0.2% ropivacaine per side halved morphine use in the 48 hours after cleft palate repair.
Mandibular nerve (V3): coronoid notch approach

Covers the lower jaw and teeth, the front two-thirds of the tongue, the floor of the mouth, the temple and the front of the ear, and relaxes the muscles of mastication. Used for jaw and tongue surgery and in the pain clinic (trigeminal neuralgia).

The needle enters in the coronoid notch, below the middle of the zygomatic arch, perpendicular to the skin, to the lateral pterygoid plate. It is then walked off the back of the plate for V3, or the front of it (towards the pterygopalatine fossa) for V2.
Aspirate often: the maxillary artery is in the way. The pharynx is just medial.
RISK	WHY
Intravascular injection, haematoma	Maxillary artery and pterygoid venous plexus. Arterial blood from here goes to the brain: small volumes can cause seizures.
Spread into the orbit	From the pterygopalatine fossa through the inferior orbital fissure: transient diplopia or visual loss (V2).
Subarachnoid spread	Rare: a needle advanced too far, towards the foramen ovale or the skull base.
Pharyngeal puncture	A needle advanced too deep, medial to the pterygoid plate.

General complications of head and neck blocks: high spinal or brainstem anaesthesia; intravascular injection and toxicity (0.5 ml or less into an artery can cause a seizure); bruising; and airway problems from block of the phrenic or recurrent laryngeal nerves.

us:
STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

Probe transverse along the eyebrow, over the upper orbital rim. Slide medially and laterally until the bright bone line has a gap: the supraorbital notch or foramen, usually in line with the pupil.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

Skin, fat, the thin frontalis and orbicularis oculi, then the bright frontal bone with its shadow. The supraorbital artery pulses at the notch (colour Doppler); the nerve lies beside it.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

In-plane from lateral (or out-of-plane), a fine needle to the tissue just over the notch. Do not enter the foramen.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

1–2 ml. Then press on the site. For the supratrochlear nerve, add 1 ml just medial, at the bridge of the nose (or fan medially from the same puncture).
